etymology: A pun on fortnight (two weeks) and fort. Epic Games released Fortnite: Save the World, a co-op game of building forts against storm-spawned monsters, in July 2017; the free Battle Royale mode followed in September 2017 and swallowed the culture. A hundred players skydive onto an island, scavenge weapons, build walls and ramps, and fight until one player or team remains, while a deadly storm shrinks the map. Rated T for Teen, it became the playground language of the late 2010s and 2020s — dances, skins, crossover events (a 2020 in-game concert drew more than twelve million players at once), and a whole vocabulary that younger siblings learned before they could play.
biblical_def: To Gen Alpha, Fortnite is the game — the place where you drop onto an island, build forts, fight, dance, and try to be the last one standing before the storm closes in. Its words fill the playground: skins, V-Bucks, emotes, cranking 90s, Victory Royale. The Christian observation: strip away the cartoon violence and the cash shop, and Fortnite is built around a picture Jesus Himself used. Everyone is building against a coming storm. Jesus said the wise man built his house upon a rock, "and the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock" (Mat 7:25). Fortnite’s forts are thrown up in seconds and always fall; the storm always wins in the end. Scripture tells a child where the fort that cannot fall is: "The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer" (Psa 18:2); "The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe" (Pro 18:10). The game’s other lessons need watching: hours that vanish, shops that pull at the wallet, and a win that requires eliminating everyone else. A father can tell a five-year-old: "In Fortnite people build forts that fall down. Jesus says the strongest house is built on Him, like a house on a big rock. When storms come, we’re safe with Him."
webster_summary: Epic Games’ battle-royale phenomenon (2017): build, fight, last one standing as the storm closes — a game that pictures, without knowing it, Christ’s parable of the house built against the storm.
webster_full: FORTNITE, proper n. (Epic Games, 2017–present; Gen Alpha usage) The free battle-royale game of building and fighting; by extension its whole culture of skins, dances, and events. "Wanna play Fortnite after dinner?"
Vocabulary it spread: drop, loot, storm, build, skin, emote, V-Bucks, battle pass, Victory Royale, default, bot, sweat.
Modes: Battle Royale, Zero Build (no building, 2022), creator-made islands.
Decode for parents: rated Teen; the violence is cartoonish, but the cash shop and time-sink are real, and voice chat with strangers is on by default for many accounts.
Webster 1828, the root — FORTNIGHT, n. The space of fourteen days; two weeks.
scriptures: Mat 7:25
And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.
Mat 7:26
And every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand:
Psa 18:2
The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower.
The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
Eph 5:16
Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
corruption_summary: Fortnite builds a culture on forts that fall, a storm that always wins, and a crown for whoever eliminates everyone else; Scripture names the Rock that does not fall and redeems the hours the island devours.
corruption_paragraphs: The game is less a single danger than a whole ecosystem: a battle that rewards eliminating every other player, a shop that rotates daily to manufacture urgency, an endless churn of seasons that never lets a child finish, and voice chat that lets strangers into the living room. Each piece is small; together they shape what a child loves and how he spends the afternoon. The foolish man of Matthew 7 is not wicked; he is busy building on sand (Mat 7:26).

The redemption is in the picture the game cannot help painting. Every round is a race to build shelter before a storm. Teach your child the parable whenever he talks about the storm; teach him Psalm 18 and Proverbs 18:10. Then govern the time — set the limits, keep the chat off, play a round with him. A father who builds on the Rock can teach his son to see through the island to the real storm and the real shelter.
roots_summary: Fortnight + fort → Fortnite: Save the World (July 2017) → Battle Royale (September 2017) → Gen Alpha’s playground language.
roots_lines: Old English feowertyne niht — fourteen nights → fortnight
Latin fortis (strong) → French fort — a stronghold
July 2017: Fortnite: Save the World — forts against storm monsters
September 2017: free Battle Royale mode; a cultural phenomenon by 2018
2020s: crossover events, Zero Build (2022), creator islands
usage: "I got second place — the storm got me right at the end."
The wise man built upon a rock; the Fortnite fort is built on sand (Mat 7:25-26).
The name of the LORD is a strong tower — the fort that does not get edited down (Pro 18:10).

etymology: Fortnite‘s in-game currency: bucks with a V usually explained by fans as Vindertech, a fictional company in Save the World; bought with real money in fixed bundles (roughly a thousand V-Bucks for under ten dollars) or by gift card, and spent on skins, emotes, and the battle pass. In December 2022 the U.S. Federal Trade Commission announced a $520 million settlement with Epic Games, including $245 million in refunds over design patterns that led players — many of them children — into unwanted purchases. "Can I get V-Bucks?" is the Fortnite household’s standard request.
biblical_def: V-Bucks are Fortnite money, and Gen Alpha children want them for one main reason: to look different from everyone else — a new skin, a new dance. A child without V-Bucks is a "default"; a child with them can be anybody. The Christian observation: the prophet asked a question that fits every cash shop: "Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not?" (Isa 55:2). A skin bought on Monday is old by Friday, because the shop rotates every day to make sure of it. Jesus warned, "Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth" (Luk 12:15), and "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt" (Mat 6:19) — and where an account can be closed. Scripture is not against spending; it is against spending without wisdom: "There is treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man spendeth it up" (Pro 21:20). A father can tell a five-year-old: "V-Bucks are pretend money that costs real money. We can use a little for fun, but God gives us money to take care of people, so we always give some away first."
webster_summary: Fortnite’s real-money currency (2017; FTC $520 million settlement, 2022) spent mostly on looks — money for "that which is not bread," and a classroom for wisdom in spending.
webster_full: V-BUCKS, n. (Fortnite currency, 2017–present; Gen Alpha usage) Virtual money bought with real money and spent on skins, emotes, and passes. "I’ve been saving my V-Bucks for the new skin."
The shop rotates daily, so items appear and disappear — a deliberate pull of urgency.
December 2022: FTC settlement with Epic Games over children’s privacy and unwanted-purchase design ($520 million total).
Decode for parents: lock purchases behind a parental PIN; most of what V-Bucks buy is appearance.
scriptures: Isa 55:2

Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.
And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
Mat 6:19
Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
There is treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man spendeth it up.
corruption_summary: V-Bucks sell children a new look that a rotating shop guarantees will be old by Friday; Scripture asks why we spend for that which is not bread and teaches the wise to keep oil in the dwelling.
corruption_paragraphs: A cash shop built for children is engineered around the weaknesses of children: urgency (the item leaves tomorrow), comparison (everyone saw your skin), and the fear of being a default. The federal government found that some of Fortnite’s purchase design crossed the line into tricking kids. Even where it does not, the system is a school of the eye that is never satisfied (Ecc 1:8).

Turn it into a school of stewardship. Let V-Bucks come from earned money; make the child wait a week before buying; give first. Ask him what he bought last month and whether he still uses it. A boy who learns at ten that the shop is designed to make him want things he will not care about by Friday has learned a lesson that will guard his paycheck at thirty.
roots_summary: V + bucks → V-Bucks (Fortnite, 2017) → FTC settlement over purchase design (December 2022).
roots_lines: American English buck — a dollar
V — by common fan account, Vindertech of Save the World
2017: V-Bucks introduced with Fortnite
Daily-rotating item shop; battle pass priced in V-Bucks
December 2022: FTC settlement, $245 million in refunds for unwanted purchases
usage: "If I do the dishes all week, can I get the V-Bucks card?"
Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? (Isa 55:2).
The wise keep oil in the dwelling; the foolish spend it up at the item shop (Pro 21:20).

etymology: A seasonal paid reward track in a video game: buy the pass, then play to unlock tiers of skins, emotes, and currency before the season ends, after which the unearned rewards are gone. The format grew from Dota 2‘s tournament "Compendium" (2013) and "Battle Pass" (2016) and was made famous by Fortnite, which added a battle pass in its second season (December 2017); nearly every major game copied it. For Gen Alpha, "Did you get the battle pass?" is a question asked at the start of every season.
biblical_def: A battle pass is a ticket you buy at the start of a game season; then you play and play to unlock prizes before the season ends and the prizes vanish. Gen Alpha kids feel its pull in their bones — "I have to get to tier 100 before Friday!" The Christian observation: the battle pass is a cleverly built machine of urgency and reward, and it trains a child to labor for a crown that is designed to disappear. Paul knew the athletes of his day did the same: "they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible" (1Co 9:25). The world’s rewards are on a season clock: "the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever" (1Jn 2:17). And the eye that grinds for the next tier is never filled: "the eye is not satisfied with seeing" (Ecc 1:8). There is a reward track that does not expire: Paul looked forward to "a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day" (2Ti 4:8). A father can tell a five-year-old: "Game prizes go away when the season ends. God’s prizes last forever — like the joy of helping someone, or knowing Jesus." And he can set a rule the pass is designed to break: the season ends when it ends, and nobody in this house grinds past bedtime to beat it.
webster_summary: Seasonal paid reward track (Dota 2, 2013–16; Fortnite, December 2017) whose prizes expire with the season — labor for a corruptible crown, against the crown that does not fade.
webster_full: BATTLE PASS, n. (game monetization, 2010s–present; Gen Alpha usage) A purchased seasonal track of unlockable rewards that expires at season’s end. "I need to grind to tier 100 before the battle pass ends."
Vocabulary: tier, XP, season, free pass / premium pass, grind.
Decode for parents: the expiring rewards are designed to make children play more, and feel loss if they stop.
Webster 1828, the root — BATTLE, n. A fight, or encounter between enemies, or opposing armies; an engagement.
scriptures: And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.
And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.
Ecc 1:8
All things are full of labour; man cannot utter it: the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.
corruption_summary: The battle pass harnesses urgency and loss-aversion to keep children grinding for crowns designed to expire; Scripture sets before them the incorruptible crown.
corruption_paragraphs: The genius of the battle pass is that it turns a game into an obligation. The child has paid; the clock is running; the rewards he has not earned will be lost forever. That is fear of missing out installed as a game mechanic, and its fruit is anxiety, late nights, and the feeling that rest is failure.

Scripture does not condemn games, but it measures their crowns. Corruptible crowns are fine as play and ruinous as masters. Teach your child to let a season go; praise him for quitting a grind; and talk about the crown that the Lord gives "unto all them also that love his appearing" (2Ti 4:8). The reward worth laboring for does not have an end date.
roots_summary: Dota 2 Compendium (2013) and Battle Pass (2016) → Fortnite battle pass (December 2017) → industry-wide seasonal reward tracks.
roots_lines: Old French bataille → English battle; Latin passus → pass, a permit or ticket
2013: Dota 2 tournament Compendium; 2016: Dota 2 Battle Pass
December 2017: Fortnite’s battle pass, season 2
Late 2010s–2020s: copied by nearly every major live-service game
usage: "I’m only on tier 62 and the season ends Thursday!"
They do it for a corruptible crown; we for an incorruptible (1Co 9:25).
The world passeth away — every season of it (1Jn 2:17).

etymology: A back-formation from emotion; as a verb ("to emote," to show emotion theatrically) it dates to early-twentieth-century American theater slang. Online, early text games (MUDs, 1990s) gave players an "emote" command for describing actions, and later online games turned emotes into animated gestures. Fortnite (2017) made emotes into dances — the Floss, the Default Dance, the Griddy — several copied from celebrities and viral videos, prompting lawsuits in 2018–19 that were dropped or dismissed. Gen Alpha uses "emote" for the dances themselves and "emoting on" someone for dancing over a defeated opponent.
biblical_def: In Gen Alpha usage an emote is a game dance or gesture, and children do them in real life at recess. "Emoting on" someone means dancing over a player you just beat — a taunt. The Christian observation: dancing and gesture are part of God’s good world. "To every thing there is a season... a time to mourn, and a time to dance" (Ecc 3:1, 4), and David "danced before the LORD with all his might" (2Sa 6:14). Joy that bursts out of the body is not a sin. But the taunting emote turns joy into mockery, and Scripture names that, too: "Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise" (Mic 7:8). The test of an emote is the test of the heart — is it gladness, or gloating? Paul’s rule for the whole body applies to dances: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep" (Rom 12:15). A father can tell a five-year-old: "It’s fun to do a happy dance! But we don’t dance to make someone feel bad when they lose. We dance because we’re glad — and the best reason to be glad is God."
webster_summary: Game gesture or dance (MUD command, 1990s; Fortnite dances, 2017-) — the body’s joy, good in its season, sinful when it becomes a taunt over the fallen.
webster_full: EMOTE, n. / v. (theater slang, early 20th c.; game usage 1990s–present; Gen Alpha usage) An animated dance or gesture performed by a game character; to perform one. "I have the Floss emote."
Emote on (someone) — to dance over a defeated player as a taunt.
Older sense: to display emotion theatrically ("the actor emoted wildly").
Decode for parents: harmless as dance; watch for the taunt.
scriptures: Ecc 3:4
A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod.
Mic 7:8
Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me.
Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
corruption_summary: The emote is the body’s joy put on a button; it is good in its season and turns sour when it becomes a dance over a defeated neighbor.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wrong with a happy dance, and much right with it. The corruption is the culture of the taunt — emoting on the fallen, celebrating another’s defeat with the body. Games reward it because it feels powerful, and children carry it onto the field. Proverbs warns against gladness at a stumble; Micah gives the fallen man’s reply.

Keep the dances and train the heart. Make the family rule that we celebrate our win and help the loser up. Teach the child that David’s dance was before the LORD, not over Michal. The best emote is gratitude moving the feet.
roots_summary: Emotion → back-formation emote (early 20th-c. theater slang) → MUD emote command (1990s) → Fortnite dance emotes (2017).
roots_lines: Latin emovere, to move out, stir up → emotion
Early 20th-c. American theater: to emote, to act out feeling
1990s text games: the emote command
2017-: Fortnite dance emotes; 2018–19 lawsuits over copied dances
Gen Alpha: emote on, to taunt by dancing
usage: "He eliminated me and then emoted on me. Rude."
A time to dance — not over the fallen (Ecc 3:4; Mic 7:8).
David danced before the LORD; that is the best emote (2Sa 6:14).

etymology: From the older English default (failure, lack) through computing’s default setting (the option chosen when no other is). In Fortnite, the default skins are the plain characters every new or non-paying player wears; by 2018 "default" had become a schoolyard insult for a kid who had not bought skins — a newbie, a poor player, a nobody. Newspapers reported children begging parents for V-Bucks so they would not be bullied as "defaults". The word spread to Roblox (see bacon hair) and to everyday use for anyone plain or unremarkable.
biblical_def: To call a kid a default is to say he has nothing — no skin, no style, no money — just the plain character everyone starts with. It is one of the cruelest little words on the Gen Alpha playground, because it marks a child by what his parents did not buy. The Christian observation: the old English meaning of the word tells the truth about all of us. Webster defined default as "a failing, or failure; an omission of that which ought to be done" — and by that measure every one of us is a default: "For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God" (Rom 3:23). No one is born with a better skin; all our righteousnesses "are as filthy rags" (Isa 64:6). The gospel is that God does not leave us in our default. He clothes us: "he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness" (Isa 61:10); "as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ" (Gal 3:27). And He looks on the heart, not the outfit (1Sa 16:7). A father can tell a five-year-old: "God doesn’t care if you have a fancy skin. Everybody starts out needing Jesus, and Jesus gives us the best clothes of all — He makes us His." And to the child doing the mocking: the default kid is the one you sit with.
webster_summary: Fortnite’s free starter skin turned schoolyard insult (2018) for a kid with nothing bought — and, in its old sense of failure, a true word for every sinner whom Christ clothes in His righteousness.
webster_full: DEFAULT, n. / a. (Gen Alpha slang, 2018–present, from Fortnite) A player wearing a free starter skin; hence, a newbie, a poor player, or a plain, unremarkable person. "He’s just a default."
Related: default skin, default dance (the starter emote), bacon hair (Roblox equivalent).
Computing sense: the setting used when no other is chosen.
Decode for parents: the insult is about money; it is a status word and often a bullying word.

Webster 1828, the root — DEFAULT, n. A failing, or failure; an omission of that which ought to be done; neglect to do what duty or law requires; as, this evil has happened through the governors default A default or fault, may be a crime, a vice, or a mere defect, according to the nature of the duty omitted.
scriptures: Rom 3:23
For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;
Isa 64:6
But we are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags; and we all do fade as a leaf; and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away.

I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels.
Gal 3:27
For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ.

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
corruption_summary: Default mocks the child who has not bought a better look; the gospel says every soul is a default in the old sense — a failure — and that Christ alone clothes the naked in righteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: The insult is respect of persons in its most childish form: a ranking by purchased appearance. Its bite is real; children have been shunned and taunted for being defaults, and parents have spent money to make it stop. A household that never names the sin will see its children either suffer it or practice it.

The word’s old meaning is the better sermon. Default is failure, falling short, the omission of what ought to be done — the state of every child of Adam. Grace does not upgrade our skin; it gives us a new one. Tell your children that God’s people all started as defaults and were clothed by the King, and they will have no reason left to mock the plain kid on the bus.
roots_summary: Old French defaute (lack, failure) → English default → computing default setting → Fortnite default skin → playground insult (2018).
roots_lines: Latin de + fallere (to deceive, fail) → Old French defaute
English default — failure, omission, want
20th-c. computing: the default setting
2017–2018: Fortnite default skins; "default" as insult
Spread to Roblox and general slang: plain, unremarkable
usage: "Don’t call him a default. Some of us just don’t have V-Bucks."
All have sinned and come short — we are all defaults (Rom 3:23).
He hath covered me with the robe of righteousness — the only skin that matters (Isa 61:10).

etymology: The free starter emote in Fortnite (2017): a goofy arm-swinging, side-to-side step every player owns. Its look is widely traced to a dance the actor Donald Faison did on the sitcom Scrubs (2000s), and Faison has joked about it. Because every player had it, the Default Dance became the most-done Fortnite move in real life — after goals, in hallways, at weddings — and "hit the default" a Gen Alpha phrase.
biblical_def: The Default Dance is the silly Fortnite dance everyone has, and Gen Alpha kids do it everywhere — after scoring, after a good grade, in the grocery line. It is a dance of pure goofiness. The Christian observation: this is one of the harmless joys, and a household can enjoy it. Scripture is full of dancing for gladness: Miriam took a timbrel "and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances" (Exo 15:20); the Psalmist says, "Let them praise his name in the dance" (Psa 149:3); and when the prodigal son came home, his elder brother heard "musick and dancing" (Luk 15:25). God Himself is pictured rejoicing over His people: "he will joy over thee with singing" (Zep 3:17). A dance the whole family can do badly together is a small sacrament of gladness. The only caution is the one every dance carries: celebrate without gloating, and do not dance on the fallen (Mic 7:8). A father can tell a five-year-old: "Let’s do the default dance — God likes happy hearts! When the lost son came home, they danced, and that’s what heaven does when people come to Jesus." Then he does it with her, badly, on purpose.
webster_summary: Fortnite’s free starter dance (2017), traced to Donald Faison on Scrubs — a harmless goofy joy, the kind of gladness Scripture invites into the dance.
webster_full: DEFAULT DANCE, n. (Fortnite starter emote, 2017–present; Gen Alpha usage) The free arm-swinging dance every player owns; done in real life as a celebration. "He scored and hit the default dance."
Hit the default — to do the dance.
Decode for parents: about as innocent as slang gets.

Webster 1828, the root — DANCE, v.i. Primarily, to leap or spring; hence, to leap or move with measured steps, regulated by a tune, sung or played on a musical instrument; to leap or step with graceful motions of the body, corresponding with the sound of the voice or an instrument.
scriptures: And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances.
Let them praise his name in the dance: let them sing praises unto him with the timbrel and harp.
Now his elder son was in the field: and as he came and drew nigh to the house, he heard musick and dancing.
Zep 3:17
The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing.
corruption_summary: The Default Dance is near-innocent goofiness; its only danger is the old one of every celebration — gloating over the one who lost.
corruption_paragraphs: There is little here to correct. The dance’s history includes a dispute over who owns a step, and its game setting includes emoting on defeated players, but the move itself, done in a kitchen, is simply silly joy. Christians who forbid every playground dance may be teaching their children that holiness is joylessness, which it is not.

Use it. Dance with your children; tell them Miriam and David danced; tell them heaven rejoices over one sinner that repents. Joy is a fruit of the Spirit, and goofiness shared is a gift. Just keep the rule: we dance for gladness, not over anyone.
roots_summary: Donald Faison’s Scrubs dance (2000s) → Fortnite Default Dance emote (2017) → real-life celebration move.
roots_lines: Old French dancer → English dance
2000s: Donald Faison’s dance on Scrubs, widely cited as the source
2017: Fortnite’s free Default Dance emote
2018-: done after goals, in hallways, at weddings; "hit the default"
usage: "I got a hundred on my spelling test!" (hits the default dance)
Let them praise his name in the dance — even the goofy one (Psa 149:3).
There was music and dancing when the prodigal came home (Luk 15:25).

etymology: The banner that appears in Fortnite (from 2017) when a player or team is the last one standing: "#1 VICTORY ROYALE," from battle royale — the genre name taken from the Japanese novel and film Battle Royale (1999, 2000), in which students are forced to fight until one survives — and victory. The phrase became a boast on playgrounds and in parody songs ("Chug Jug With You," 2018), and Gen Alpha uses it for any win, from a spelling bee to beating a sibling at Uno.
biblical_def: A Victory Royale is the Fortnite win — the prize for being the last player left. To a Gen Alpha child, "I got a Victory Royale!" is the proudest sentence in the language. The Christian observation: children are right to love victory; God made us for it, and Scripture is full of it. But the battle-royale kind of victory is won by being the only one left. Christ’s victory is the opposite. He won by losing — by dying — and His win brings "many sons unto glory" (Heb 2:10) instead of eliminating them. "But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ" (1Co 15:57). His people share it: "in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us" (Rom 8:37), and "this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith" (1Jn 5:4). The King’s victory is a royal victory indeed, and its crown is shared. A father can tell a five-year-old: "In the game, only one person wins. When Jesus won over sin and death, He made a way for everybody who trusts Him to win too. That’s the best victory royale." And when his child wins anything, he can teach the first words of a Christian victor: "thanks be to God."
webster_summary: Fortnite’s last-one-standing win banner (2017, from the battle royale genre) — a victory won by eliminating all others, set against Christ’s victory that brings many sons unto glory.
webster_full: VICTORY ROYALE, n. (Fortnite, 2017–present; Gen Alpha usage) A win in Fortnite’s battle royale — last player or team standing; by extension, any triumph. "Victory Royale! I beat you at Uno!"
From battle royale (the genre, after the Japanese Battle Royale, 1999–2000) + victory.
Decode for parents: harmless as a boast; a good hook for teaching what kind of victory Christ won.

Webster 1828, the root — VICTORY, n. Conquest; the defeat of an enemy in battle, or of an antagonist in contest; a gaining of the superiority in war or combat. victory supposes the power of an enemy or an antagonist to prove inferior to that of the victor. victory however depends not always on superior skill or valor; it is often gained by the fault or mistake of the vanquished.
Webster 1828, the root — ROYAL, a. Kingly; pertaining to a king; regal; as royal power or prerogative; a royal garden; royal domains; the royal family.
scriptures: But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Rom 8:37
Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us.
For whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world: and this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith.
Heb 2:10
For it became him, for whom are all things, and by whom are all things, in bringing many sons unto glory, to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings.
corruption_summary: The Victory Royale is won by being the only one left; Christ’s victory is won by dying for others and is shared with all who believe.
corruption_paragraphs: The genre’s premise is stark: a hundred enter, one leaves. A culture that plays it daily absorbs a picture of winning as elimination — your victory is everyone else’s loss. That is the logic of pride and rivalry, and children carry it into classrooms and sports.

The gospel’s victory is royal in a different way. The King laid down His life; His triumph over sin and death is given away to the losers; and His people overcome by faith. Let your child enjoy a win, and teach him to say "thanks be to God," to shake the other hand, and to remember that the best victory in history made many winners.
roots_summary: Japanese Battle Royale (novel 1999, film 2000) → battle-royale game genre → Fortnite’s "#1 Victory Royale" (2017).
roots_lines: Latin victoria → English victory; French royale, royal
Old English sense of battle royal — a fight among many until one remains
1999–2000: Koushun Takami’s Battle Royale novel and film
2017: Fortnite’s win banner "#1 Victory Royale"
2018: "Chug Jug With You" parody; playground boast
usage: "Victory Royale! Me and Dad won the duo round!"
Thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory — say that after the win (1Co 15:57).
His victory brings many sons unto glory; nobody is eliminated who comes to Him (Heb 2:10).

etymology: Fortnite building slang from competitive play around 2018–19: a rapid sequence of wall, ramp, and floor placed while turning ninety degrees, repeated to climb high above an opponent in seconds. "Cranking" (turning hard, as with a crank) plus 90s (the ninety-degree turns). Mastering 90s took hours of practice in creative mode, and "he can crank 90s" became a mark of skill; the phrase outlived its technical meaning as kid slang for doing anything fast and well. Fortnite added a no-building mode, Zero Build, in March 2022.
biblical_def: Cranking 90s is a fast Fortnite building trick — spinning and stacking ramps and walls to rise above the other player. Gen Alpha kids practice it for hours and brag about speed. The Christian observation: the boast underneath is a boast about skill earned by practice, and Scripture honors that. "Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings" (Pro 22:29). Bezaleel was filled with skill for craftsmanship; the Levite musicians were "skilful"; diligence in small things is a virtue the Bible praises again and again. But Scripture also ranks practice: "bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things" (1Ti 4:8). A boy who can crank 90s in his sleep but has never memorized a psalm has practiced the lesser thing. And building has its own warning in the gospel: count the cost before you build a tower (Luk 14:28), and build on the Rock, not on sand (Mat 7:24). A father can tell a five-year-old: "It takes lots of practice to build fast in a game. God wants us to practice good things too — like saying kind words and learning Bible verses — so we get really good at them."
webster_summary: Fortnite building technique (c. 2018–19): rapid stacked ramps and walls on ninety-degree turns — practiced skill Scripture honors, ranked below the practice of godliness.
webster_full: CRANKING 90s, v. phr. (Fortnite competitive slang, c. 2018–present) Building rapidly upward with repeated wall-ramp placements on ninety-degree turns. "He cranked 90s and got high ground."
Related: high ground, box up, edit, sweat (a highly skilled, intense player).
Extended kid usage: doing something very fast and skillfully.
Decode for parents: a sign of hours of practice — worth knowing how many.

Webster 1828, the root — CRANK, n. Literally, a bend or turn. Hence, an iron axis with the end bent like an elbow, for moving a piston, the saw in a saw-mill, etc., and causing it to rise and fall at every turn.
scriptures: Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.
For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?
Mat 7:24
Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:
corruption_summary: Cranking 90s is skill bought by practice, which Scripture honors; the danger is practicing the lesser thing to the neglect of godliness, which profits in all things.
corruption_paragraphs: There is honest discipline in a child who drills a hard skill until his hands know it. The question is where the discipline is going. Many Gen Alpha boys have logged more practice hours on Fortnite builds than on any instrument, sport, or book, and the game is designed to reward exactly that devotion.

Praise the diligence and redirect some of it. Ask your son what he can practice that will last — a verse, a skill with his hands, a kindness repeated until it is habit. Bodily exercise profits a little; Fortnite exercise profits less; godliness profits in all things.
roots_summary: English crank (to turn) + 90s (ninety-degree turns) → competitive Fortnite building (2018–19) → kid slang for fast skill.
roots_lines: Old English cranc — a bent handle for turning → to crank
2018–19: competitive Fortnite building technique
Practiced in creative mode; a mark of skill on the playground
March 2022: Zero Build mode removes building for some players
usage: "Watch me crank 90s — I practiced for like three hours."
Seest thou a child diligent in his building? Now teach him to practice godliness (Pro 22:29; 1Ti 4:8).
Count the cost before you build the tower (Luk 14:28).

etymology: From English box. In Fortnite, "boxing up" means walling yourself into a four-sided shelter, and a "box fight" is a close-range battle inside or around those walls; to get boxed is to be trapped in one and eliminated. Around 2019–20 the taunt "boxed like a fish" spread through Fortnite videos and playgrounds as a nonsense rhyme for a humiliating defeat, and "you got boxed" became general kid slang for being thoroughly beaten. The older boxing sense — to strike with the fist — runs alongside it.
biblical_def: To get boxed in Gen Alpha slang is to get trapped and beaten — in Fortnite, closed in by walls with no way out; on the playground, outplayed completely. "You just got boxed like a fish!" is the taunt. The Christian observation: the feeling the word names is real, and Scripture speaks to it often — being hemmed in, cornered, with no way out. David prayed from that place and testified: "thou hast not shut me up into the hand of the enemy: thou hast set my feet in a large room" (Psa 31:8), and "He brought me forth also into a large place; he delivered me, because he delighted in me" (Psa 18:19). The trapped bird is Israel’s picture of rescue: "Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped" (Psa 124:7). And for the child boxed in by temptation, there is a promise: God "will with the temptation also make a way to escape" (1Co 10:13). A father can tell a five-year-old: "When you feel stuck, like you’re in a box, you can pray. God always knows the way out, and He likes to bring us to wide-open places." The taunt itself needs the usual rule: we can win, but we do not mock the boxed.
webster_summary: Fortnite slang for being walled in and eliminated ("boxed like a fish," c. 2019–20) — the cornered feeling Scripture answers with the God who sets our feet in a large room.
webster_full: BOXED, a. / pp. (Fortnite slang, c. 2018–present; Gen Alpha usage) Trapped inside built walls and eliminated; hence, thoroughly beaten. "He got boxed like a fish."
Related: box up (to wall oneself in), box fight, boxed like a fish (taunt).
Older senses: placed in a box; struck with the fist.
Decode for parents: harmless gamer talk, often with a taunt attached.
Webster 1828, the root — BOX, n. The quantity that a box contains; as a box of quicksilver; a box or rings.
scriptures: Psa 31:8
And hast not shut me up into the hand of the enemy: thou hast set my feet in a large room.
He brought me forth also into a large place; he delivered me, because he delighted in me.
Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped.

There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.
corruption_summary: Boxed names the cornered defeat and usually mocks it; Scripture names the same corner and shows the God who breaks the snare and brings His children into a large place.
corruption_paragraphs: The slang is light, but the taunt attached to it is the ordinary playground sin of mocking the loser. "Boxed like a fish" is a rhyme meant to humiliate. Children who learn to laugh at the trapped can grow into adults who do not help them.

The feeling of being boxed is worth taking seriously. Children feel cornered by bullies, by failure, by their own sins. Teach them Psalm 18:19 and 1 Corinthians 10:13 — there is always a way of escape, and the Lord loves to bring His people out into the wide places. A word about a game can become a word about rescue.
roots_summary: Latin buxus (boxwood) → English box → Fortnite box up / box fight → boxed, "boxed like a fish" (c. 2019–20).
roots_lines: Latin buxus / Greek pyxis — boxwood, a box
English to box — to enclose in a box; separately, to strike with the fist
Fortnite: box up, box fight, boxed
c. 2019–20: the taunt "boxed like a fish"
usage: "You got boxed like a fish!" "Okay, okay, rematch."
He brought me forth also into a large place — un-boxed (Psa 18:19).
With the temptation God makes a way to escape — every box has a door (1Co 10:13).

etymology: A dance in which the arms swing side to side in front of and behind the body while the hips swing the other way, like pulling dental floss. Popularized by Russell Horning, "the Backpack Kid," in a 2016 Instagram video and made famous when he danced it beside Katy Perry on Saturday Night Live in May 2017; Fortnite made it an emote in 2018 and the floss became the worldwide schoolyard dance of that year (some schools banned it in class). Horning sued Epic Games in December 2018 and later dropped the suit. Older senses of floss: silk fibers, and (1990s hip-hop) to show off.
biblical_def: The floss is the arm-swinging dance that every Gen Alpha child of 2018 could do, and many still do — at recess, at weddings, in the cereal aisle. It is pure silly motion. The Christian observation: like most children’s dances, it is one of the small joys, and joy is God’s idea. "Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing" (Psa 30:11), and a whole people sang that God would "joy over thee with singing" (Zep 3:17). Children who move their bodies in delight are doing something their Creator made them to do. There is one older slang sense a parent should know: in 1990s hip-hop, to floss meant to show off wealth — flashy jewelry, cars — and Scripture has a word for that, too: "Let not the rich man glory in his riches: but let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me" (Jer 9:23-24). The Gen Alpha floss is the dance, not the boast. A father can tell a five-year-old: "Show me your floss! God made your arms and your legs and your happy heart — you can dance for Him." The father who learns the floss badly is giving his daughter a memory and a laugh, which are gifts too.
webster_summary: The arm-swinging dance of the Backpack Kid (2016; SNL 2017; Fortnite 2018) — harmless joy in motion; its older hip-hop sense, to show off wealth, is the one Jeremiah rebukes.
webster_full: FLOSS, n. / v. (dance, 2016–present; Gen Alpha usage) A dance of swinging arms and counter-swinging hips; to do the dance. "She can floss so fast."
1990s hip-hop sense: to floss, to flaunt wealth (still heard in older rap).
Original sense: silk fibers; dental floss, the thread for cleaning teeth.
Decode for parents: the dance is harmless; the show-off sense is the one worth a talk.
Webster 1828, the root — FLOSS, n. A downy or silky substance in the husks of certain plants.
scriptures: Thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing: thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness;
Zep 3:17
The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing.
Jer 9:23
Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches:
Jer 9:24

But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: The floss dance is harmless joy; the older slang sense — to floss, to flaunt wealth — is the boast of the rich man Jeremiah forbids.
corruption_paragraphs: Children’s dance crazes come and go, and the floss is among the most innocent: no lyrics, no gesture beyond silliness. The only real ground for caution is the word’s other life in hip-hop, where flossing meant displaying jewelry and money — the glory in riches that Scripture names as vain.

Enjoy the dance, and teach the distinction. We dance because we are glad, not to show what we own. If the child ever hears "flossin’" in a song about money, tell her Jeremiah’s word: glory in knowing God.
roots_summary: Old French flosche (down, nap) → English floss (silk fiber, dental floss) → 1990s hip-hop floss (to show off) → the Backpack Kid’s dance (2016–18).
roots_lines: Old French flosche — down, soft fibers → English floss
19th c.: dental floss
1990s hip-hop: to floss, to flaunt wealth
2016–2017: Russell Horning’s dance; SNL with Katy Perry (May 2017)
2018: Fortnite emote; worldwide schoolyard craze
usage: "Bet you can’t floss for a whole minute."
Thou hast turned my mourning into dancing — even the floss (Psa 30:11).
Floss with your arms, not with your riches (Jer 9:23-24).

etymology: A touchdown dance of quick heel-taps with the hands making goggles around the eyes, named for its creator Allen "Griddy" Davis, a high-school friend of the football star Justin Jefferson in Louisiana. Jefferson spread it at LSU (2019) and in the NFL (2020-), and it became the celebration of the early 2020s from pro fields to Pee Wee leagues; Fortnite sold it as an emote ("Get Griddy") in 2022. "Hit the griddy" is the Gen Alpha way to say "celebrate."
biblical_def: To hit the griddy is to do the goggle-eyed, heel-tapping touchdown dance. Gen Alpha children do it after every goal, every basket, every kickball home run. The Christian observation: celebration of a good thing done well is a gift, not a vice. Scripture tells God’s people to rejoice in their labor — "there is nothing better, than that a man should rejoice in his own works; for that is his portion" (Ecc 3:22) — and Paul turns every ordinary act into worship: "whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God" (1Co 10:31). The griddy can be gratitude with feet. Its hazards are the old ones of every end-zone dance: the celebration that is really a boast, and the dance in the opponent’s face. "Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth" (Pro 27:2). Christian athletes have shown the better way by pointing up after a score — giving the credit to the Giver. A father can tell a five-year-old: "When you do something good, you can do a happy dance — and then say ‘thank You, God,’ because He made your legs fast." And he can teach the order of a champion: celebrate, thank God, shake the other team’s hands.
webster_summary: Allen Davis’s goggle-eyed heel-tap dance, spread by Justin Jefferson (2019-) and Fortnite (2022) — celebration that can be gratitude, or a boast in the opponent’s face.
webster_full: GRIDDY, n. (dance, c. 2019–present; Gen Alpha usage) A heel-tapping celebration dance with hands forming goggles over the eyes. "He scored and hit the griddy."
Hit the griddy — to do the dance; to celebrate.
Named for Allen "Griddy" Davis; spread by Justin Jefferson (LSU 2019, NFL 2020-).
Decode for parents: harmless; the only question is whether it is gratitude or gloating.
scriptures: Ecc 3:22
Wherefore I perceive that there is nothing better, than that a man should rejoice in his own works; for that is his portion: for who shall bring him to see what shall be after him?
Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.
Pro 27:2
Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips.
Mic 7:8
Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me.
corruption_summary: The griddy is a celebration; it is good as gratitude and wrong only as gloating over the beaten opponent.
corruption_paragraphs: Sports culture has turned celebration into self-advertisement, and children imitate what they see. The griddy itself is innocent; the culture around it trains a child to make every success about himself and to perform it for an audience — or to rub it in. The Proverbs warn against self-praise; the prophets against rejoicing over the fallen.

Keep the dance, change the direction. Teach the child to celebrate with thanks, to give God glory, and to honor the team that lost. A boy who learns at seven to hit the griddy and then help the other kid up is learning to be a gracious man.
roots_summary: Allen "Griddy" Davis’s dance (Louisiana, 2010s) → Justin Jefferson at LSU (2019) and in the NFL (2020-) → Fortnite "Get Griddy" (2022) → Gen Alpha celebration.
roots_lines: Named for its creator, Allen "Griddy" Davis
2019: Justin Jefferson spreads it at LSU
2020-: NFL touchdown celebration; youth sports craze
2022: Fortnite emote "Get Griddy"
Gen Alpha: hit the griddy = celebrate
usage: "Coach said we can hit the griddy if we win, but we shake hands first."
Whatsoever ye do — even the griddy — do all to the glory of God (1Co 10:31).
Let another man praise thee; dance with thanks, not with a sneer (Pro 27:2).

etymology: From English sturdy (strong, firm, hardy). As slang, "hit the sturdy" names a stomping, knee-bouncing, shoulder-rocking dance from New York City — Bronx and Brooklyn — tied to the New York drill music scene of the early 2020s; it went viral in 2022–23 through street videos, NFL celebrations, and school hallways. Gen Alpha uses "hit the sturdy" for the dance and "sturdy" as praise for something tough or solid. Parents should know that much of the drill music the dance grew up with carries violent lyrics, while the dance itself does not.
biblical_def: To hit the sturdy is to do a heavy, stomping, bouncing dance that started in New York. Gen Alpha kids do it to celebrate, and they also use "sturdy" the way grandparents did — for something strong that will not fall over. The Christian observation: the old word is the better word, and Scripture is full of the sturdy. The man who trusts God "shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water" (Psa 1:3). Paul’s command to a church sounds like a sturdy stance: "Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong" (1Co 16:13), and to every believer: "be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might" (Eph 6:10). The strongest stance in the world is the one that stands on God: "he only is my rock and my salvation: he is my defence; I shall not be moved" (Psa 62:6). The dance’s background in drill music is a reason for a parent to know what songs a child is hearing with it; the dance itself is a stomp of joy. A father can tell a five-year-old: "Sturdy means strong, like a tree that doesn’t fall down in the wind. When we hold on to Jesus, we’re sturdy inside — the wind can’t knock us over."
webster_summary: New York stomping dance ("hit the sturdy," viral 2022–23) and praise-word for something tough — the old word for the strength Scripture locates in those who stand fast in the Lord.
webster_full: STURDY, n. / v. (New York dance, viral 2022–present; Gen Alpha usage) A stomping, knee-bouncing celebration dance. "Hit the sturdy!"
Praise sense: tough, solid, impressive. "That shot was sturdy."
Background: New York drill music scene, early 2020s.
Decode for parents: the dance is fine; know the songs it travels with.
Webster 1828, the root — STURDY, a. Hardy; stout; foolishly obstinate; implying coarseness or rudeness.
scriptures: Psa 1:3
And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.
Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
Eph 6:10
Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might.
Psa 62:6
He only is my rock and my salvation: he is my defence; I shall not be moved.
corruption_summary: The sturdy dance is a harmless stomp; the word’s real strength is the old one Scripture gives to those who stand fast in the faith and are not moved.
corruption_paragraphs: The dance carries a soundtrack. New York drill, the scene that gave it its home, is notorious for lyrics about violence and rivalry, and a child who learns a dance from a video often learns the song too. That is the only real caution, and it is a caution about music more than movement.
The word is a gift. Teach your child that sturdy is what God makes His people: rooted like the tree of Psalm 1, standing fast like Paul’s church, strong in the Lord. Then let him stomp.
roots_summary: Old French estourdi (stunned, reckless) → English sturdy (strong, firm) → New York "hit the sturdy" dance (2022–23).
roots_lines: Old French estourdi — stunned, violent, reckless
Middle English sturdi — fierce; later, strong and firm
Early 2020s: New York drill scene; "hit the sturdy"
2022–23: viral in street videos, NFL celebrations, school hallways
usage: "We won the relay and everybody hit the sturdy."
Stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong — that’s sturdy (1Co 16:13).
He only is my rock; I shall not be moved (Psa 62:6).
